name: Perl
title: Perl, the text-wrangling language
intro: Larry Wall released Perl in 1987 to pull reports out of messy text files, and it became the glue of early web servers and system administration: CGI scripts, log crunchers, build tools. Its motto is "there's more than one way to do it", and its regular expressions were so good that most other languages copied them. Variable names carry a sigil that says what they hold: $ for one value, @ for a list, % for a hash. These lessons use Perl 5, which still ships with most Linux and macOS systems. Every example is a whole script and shows exactly what it prints. To run one yourself, save it as hello.pl and type perl hello.pl.

sections.p: Start every script with use strict; and use warnings;: they make Perl complain about typos and mistakes instead of guessing. print prints exactly what it is given, so you add "\n" yourself. use feature 'say'; turns on say, which is print with the newline added.

my creates a variable. A single value, called a scalar, has a $ in front. The dot . joins strings and x repeats one. Inside double quotes a variable is replaced by its value; single quotes keep the text exactly as written.
sections.out:
Hi, Hazel!
Hazel has 7 nuts
$name has $nuts nuts
----------

options:
Up the oak
Up the oak
practice.why: Double quotes put the variable's value in. Single quotes print the text as written.
x repeats a string the given number of times. The dot just joins.

practice.q: What does use strict make Perl do?
options: Refuse variables that weren't declared with my
Print every line as it runs
practice.answer: Refuse variables that weren't declared with my
practice.why: Without it, a misspelled variable name quietly becomes a new, empty variable.

lessons.title: Numbers, strings and comparing
lessons.summary: One scalar type, two sets of comparison operators.

sections.p: A scalar can hold a number or a string, and Perl converts between them as needed: "4" + 3 is 7, and 4 . 3 is the string "43". Division gives a fraction when one is needed. int drops the fraction and % gives the remainder; ** raises to a power.

Because a scalar may be either, Perl has separate operators for comparing numbers and strings. Numbers use symbols: ==, !=, <, >. Strings use words: eq, ne, lt, gt. Picking the wrong one gives a surprising answer: as strings, "10" comes before "9", because 1 sorts before 9.
sections.out:
bigger
smaller
same number
different text

sections.p: Perl has no separate true and false values. The number 0, the strings "" and "0", and undef (no value at all) count as false; everything else is true. // gives a fallback when a value is undef.
sections.out:
'0' is false
'1' is true
'' is false
'0' is false
'0.0' is true
'nuts' is true
nothing yet

practice.why: lt compares letter by letter, and c comes before d. 100 < 20 compares numbers, and it is false.
Dot and + have the same priority and go left to right: 7 . 7 is "77", and "77" + 1 is 78.

practice.q: Which of these values is true in Perl?
practice.why: Only 0, "0", "" and undef are false. "0.0" is a non-empty string that isn't exactly "0".

sections.p: An array holds a list and its name starts with @. To read one element you write $trees[0], with a $, because one element is a scalar. push adds to the end, pop takes from the end, and scalar(@trees) counts the elements. $trees[-1] is the last one.
sections.out:
3
oak hazel
oak, ash, hazel
oak ash hazel
hazel; left: oak ash

sections.p: A hash maps keys to values and its name starts with %. One value is $stash{oak}, again with a $. A hash keeps no order, so code that prints one usually walks through sort keys %stash. exists checks whether a key is there.

sort on its own sorts as strings. For numbers, give it a block: sort { $a <=> $b }, where <=> compares two numbers. grep keeps the items whose block is true and map changes each one; inside both, $_ is the current item.

practice.why: There are three elements. Index 1 is the second one, y, and -1 is the last, z.
Plain sort compares as strings, character by character, so anything starting with 1 comes before 9.

practice.q: Why is one element of @trees written $trees[0]?
options: One element is a single scalar value
It is a typo Perl forgives
practice.answer: One element is a single scalar value
practice.why: The sigil tells you what you get back: $ for one value, @ for a list.

lessons.title: Decisions and loops
lessons.summary: if, unless, statement modifiers, foreach, last and next.

sections.p: if, elsif and else work as in other languages, and the braces are always required. unless is the opposite of if. For one short statement Perl lets you put the condition after it, which reads like English: say "feast" if $nuts > 20;.
sections.out:
good day
time to bury some

sections.p: foreach (or just for) walks a list; 1..5 is the list of numbers from 1 to 5. while repeats while its test holds. next skips to the next pass and last leaves the loop.

practice.why: The modifier form of for runs the statement once per item with $_ set, so it adds 1, 2, 3 and 4.
$cold is 0, which is false, so unless runs its statement and if does not.

sections.p: Regular expressions are where Perl shines. $text =~ /pattern/ is true when the pattern is found. \d matches a digit, \w a letter, digit or underscore, + means one or more, and brackets capture what they matched into $1, $2 and so on.
sections.out:
who: Hazel
how many: 12
mentions a day

sections.p: s/old/new/ replaces the first match; add g to replace them all, and i to ignore case. In list context a match with g returns every capture at once, which makes pulling all the numbers out of a line a one-liner.
split breaks a string apart wherever a pattern matches, and join glues a list back together. Together with a hash they turn a line of a data file into named fields.

practice.why: Without the g flag, s/// replaces only the first match.
The three brackets capture year, month and day into $1, $2 and $3, and the line prints them in reverse.

options: The letter d and a plus sign
practice.why: \d is any digit and + means one or more of the thing before it.

lessons.title: Subroutines and references
lessons.summary: sub, @_, returning lists, and nested data with references.

sections.p: sub defines a subroutine. The arguments arrive in the array @_; the usual first line copies them into named variables with my ($a, $b) = @_;. A sub can return a list, and the caller can unpack it straight into variables.

An array or hash can't sit directly inside another one, so Perl uses references: a scalar that points at the real data. [...] makes a reference to a new array and {...} to a new hash. -> follows the reference, and @{...} gets the whole list back. This is how Perl builds records and nested data.

practice.why: shift takes the first argument as the starting max, and the loop checks the rest.
Copying a reference copies the pointer, not the array. Both names point at the same array, which now has four items.

lessons.title: Reading and writing files
lessons.summary: open, readline, chomp, and the diamond operator.

sections.p: open ties a filehandle to a path. The mode '>' writes (replacing any old file), '<' reads, and '>>' appends. Always check the open with or die $!: $! holds the system error. <$in> reads one line, and chomp strips the newline.
<> reads from each file named in @ARGV, the same way a one-liner does. Inside a block you can set @ARGV for a moment with local, so a script can point the diamond at a chosen file.
Mode '>>' adds to the end. say {$log} ... prints to that handle with a newline. Reading the file back afterwards shows both lines.

practice.why: Two lines were written, and reading in list context returns one element per line.
>> appends y after x. Setting $/ to undef makes one read return the whole file.

practice.q: What does chomp do to a line read with <>?
practice.why: <> keeps the newline; chomp strips it so the string is just the text.

lessons.title: Packages and modules
lessons.summary: package names, qualified subs, and use for core modules.

sections.p: A package gives a namespace for subroutines. MathNuts::share calls share inside package MathNuts. Switching back to package main returns to the default namespace where the script began. Several packages can live in one file while you are learning; real modules usually get their own .pm file.
use List::Util qw(sum max); loads a core module and imports the named subs into the current package. After that, sum and max work like built-ins. qw(...) is just a tidy list of words.
my is private to a block. our declares a package variable that other code can reach by name. They are handy for a shared setting; for most data, passing arguments is clearer.

practice.why: Greeter::hello calls the sub in that package with Pip as $_[0].
min from List::Util returns the smallest number.

practice.q: What is the difference between my $x and our $x?
options: my is private to the block; our is a package variable others can name
They are the same under strict
practice.answer: my is private to the block; our is a package variable others can name
practice.why: our puts the name in the package symbol table; my does not.

lessons.title: Blessed objects
lessons.summary: bless, methods with ->, and a tiny class.

sections.p: Perl's classic objects are hashes (or other references) that have been blessed into a package. $class->new(...) calls new as a class method; inside it, bless $hash, $class marks the hash as belonging to that package. Afterwards $obj->add(4) calls add with the object as the first argument.
Returning $self lets the caller chain calls. Each method still receives the same blessed hash.
ref $obj gives the package name a reference was blessed into (or the plain type for an unblessed reference). A package can list parents in @ISA; method lookup walks that list.

practice.why: bless tags the hash as Box, so ref returns Box, and n reads the field.
Two bumps add 2 each; returning $s keeps the chain on one object.

options: Marks the reference as an object of that package so -> finds its methods
Copies the hash into a new class
Converts the hash into a string
practice.answer: Marks the reference as an object of that package so -> finds its methods
practice.why: That tag is what turns a plain hash reference into a Perl object.

lessons.title: Project: a nut ledger
lessons.summary: Parse lines into hashes, total with a hash, and print a table.

sections.p: This script walks a ledger of lines such as day 3: acorn x9. A regex pulls each good line into a hash; bad lines are reported and skipped. A hash of totals feeds a sorted table with percentages, and a final pass picks the biggest single find — the same shape as a small report you might write for a log file.
sections.out:
skipped line 4: cannot read "day two: acorn x3"
skipped line 7: cannot read "day 4 acorn x5"
acorn     15   68.2%
hazelnut   6   27.3%
walnut     1    4.5%
best find: 9 acorn on day 3

sections.p: Read the ledger from a file with while (<>), wrap the parser in a package Ledger with a blessed object that holds the totals, or warn when a nut name is not in a fixed list.

practice.q: Why store each entry as a hash like { day => 1, nut => "acorn", count => 6 }?
options: Named fields stay clear when you sort and total later
Hashes are the only way to store numbers
practice.answer: Named fields stay clear when you sort and total later
practice.why: $_->{count} reads better than $_->[2] once the script grows.
Count 3 ties are broken by name, so acorn before walnut, then hazel with 1.
Sorting by n descending puts 9 first, and list assignment takes that one hash.
